proposals.relationship: Borrows Cohen’s culture-of-unity formulation as a starting point for examining the racial limits of industrial union solidarity.
proposals.evidence_note: Sugrue explicitly attributes the phrase to Cohen on391 and cites Making a New Deal in note5 on392. He uses it to frame what racial division eroded and then considers Nelson’s revision. This is a specific conceptual resource rather than unqualified agreement, formal supervision or a claim that every union had achieved unity. Original Cohen book unread; note’s1989 date variant not propagated.

proposals.relationship: Uses Roediger’s work to frame racial identity and class consciousness as intertwined rather than competing explanations.
proposals.evidence_note: On394 Sugrue explicitly compares Nelson with Roediger as avoiding the sterile race-versus-class dichotomy, with notes8–9 identifying books and the1993 multiple-identities essay. Saxton/Ignatiev and Nelson retain distinct credit. This positive analytical use coexists with the following criticism; original Roediger texts unread.

proposals.relationship: Questions Roediger’s emphasis on white workers’ agency without sufficient attention to capital and the constraints of labor markets.
proposals.evidence_note: The central395 paragraph explicitly includes Roediger alongside Nelson and other labor historians in an overemphasis on workers’ ability to shape segmented labor markets. Sugrue calls for employer, market and political context while rejecting deterministic economics. The named extension applies to this agency reservation; every subsequent Nelson-specific criticism is not automatically attributed to Roediger. Positive use on394 remains.
primary_locators: Printed395, paragraph Each of these propositions; page image checked

proposals.relationship: Cites Gerstle’s examination of race and the liberal consensus when situating northern white workers’ resistance to civil-rights measures.
proposals.evidence_note: Sugrue392/n6 explicitly places Race and the Myth of the Liberal Consensus alongside his own and Hirsch’s findings on northern resistance. Note5 separately directs readers to Gerstle and others’ responses to Michael Goldfield’s1993 Race and the CIO article, not responses to Nelson. This bounded supporting reference is not formal mentoring, an exclusive framework or a claim that Gerstle authored all of Nelson’s analysis. Original Gerstle essay unread.

proposals.relationship: Cites Higginbotham’s analysis of race alongside Fields when arguing for historically specific studies of racial practices.
proposals.evidence_note: Sugrue393 makes Fields’s construction argument the explicit starting point and n7 adds Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, continuing onto394. This establishes a specific supporting resource, not a transfer of Fields’s primary credit to Higginbotham or proof of full agreement. The original article remains unread; neither an editorial tribute nor a citation-chain inference supplies the relationship.
